A temporary construct in this situation is not the final result — it's part of the overall treatment plan.
Various reconstructive techniques exist for replacing large bone defects.
Depending on the clinical situation, the following may be considered:

items: bone grafting
induced membrane technique and staged reconstruction
bone transport
internal or external fixation methods
structural reconstructive implants
individualized 3D solutions for complex defects
a combination of several methods

body.text: The choice of method depends on more than just the size of the defect. Its location, the condition of the soft tissues, infection status, mechanical conditions, and the ultimate treatment goal all matter.
We don't fit the patient to one technology — we fit the technology to the specific reconstructive task.
In complex cases, standard implants may not be enough to restore the anatomy that was lost.
Modern CT imaging and digital planning make it possible to create a three-dimensional model of the defect and plan individualized reconstructive solutions.
Where indicated, patient-specific 3D-printed implants, designed to match the specific anatomy and reconstructive task, can be used.
This approach is especially important in cases where a large defect, complex geometry, or previous operations make it impossible to achieve an optimal result with standard implants.
3D technology, however, is not an end in itself. It's one of the tools of reconstruction, used when it offers a specific clinical advantage.
We review the original injury, previous operations, any existing implants, and the results of bacteriological and other tests.
For a complex reconstructive case, the history of prior treatment is critically important.
We determine the location and size of the bone loss, the condition of the remaining bone tissue, soft tissues, and joints, and the limb's axis and length.
CT imaging and digital reconstruction are used when necessary.
We define the ultimate treatment goal and the sequence of stages.
If multi-stage treatment is needed, each stage is planned as part of a single reconstructive strategy.
The chosen method of defect replacement and stabilization is carried out according to the specific clinical situation.
After reconstruction, the loading regimen is gradually adjusted and functional recovery begins. Its duration depends on the scale of the defect and the reconstruction method chosen.

blocks.heading: We plan the entire treatment journey, not just one operation

body.text: With a critical defect, it's important to understand from the very beginning what end result we're aiming for and what role each stage plays.
Reconstruction takes more than simply filling in the missing part of the bone. It's necessary to provide both the conditions for healing and sufficient mechanical stability at the same time.

blocks.heading: We use digital planning and individualized solutions

body.text: In complex cases, CT-based reconstruction, 3D modeling, and patient-specific implants make it possible to plan reconstruction to match the specific anatomy.

blocks.heading: We assess the function of the whole limb

body.text: The ultimate goal isn't simply an unbroken line of bone on an X-ray, but a stable, weight-bearing, and as functional as possible limb.

blocks.heading: Reconstruction of a critical tibial defect with an individualized 3D implant
From major bone loss to an active life

body.text: The patient presented 3 months after a severe lower-leg injury. By the time of presentation, the soft tissues had already healed, but a significant post-traumatic tibial defect had formed.

After a comprehensive assessment of the limb, individualized reconstruction planning was carried out. A patient-specific 3D implant, with geometry adapted to the specific defect, was manufactured to replace the bone defect.
The reconstruction was aimed not only at replacing the lost section of bone, but also at restoring the limb's continuity, stability, and weight-bearing capacity.
The patient maintains a high level of physical activity and goes on mountain hikes.
The ultimate goal of complex reconstruction isn't an X-ray. It's a functional limb that allows a person to return to an active life.

blocks.heading: How large a bone defect can still be restored?

body.text: There's no single number of centimeters beyond which reconstruction automatically becomes impossible.

What matters is the location of the defect, the condition of the soft tissues, infection, the quality of the remaining bone, the condition of the joints, and the overall functional potential of the limb.

blocks.heading: If part of a bone was removed because of infection, can it be restored?

body.text: In many cases, reconstruction is possible after an infected or nonviable section of bone has been removed.
However, before definitive reconstruction it's essential to achieve control of the infectious process and prepare the tissues for the next stage.

blocks.heading: Will several operations always be necessary?

body.text: Not necessarily, but multi-stage treatment is common with large defects.
The number of operations depends on the cause of the defect, the presence of infection, the condition of the tissues, and the reconstruction method chosen.

blocks.heading: What is a spacer, and why is it placed?

body.text: A spacer is a temporary construct that may be used during one stage of treatment.
Its function depends on the specific situation: it can help temporarily fill the defect, maintain space, and serve as part of the strategy for treating an infectious process.
No.
An individualized 3D implant is just one of the possible reconstruction tools. It's used when the anatomy of the defect and the clinical task make such a solution appropriate.
In some cases — yes.
The possibility and method of restoring length depend on the size of the defect, the condition of the tissues, any deformity, and the reconstructive strategy chosen.

blocks.heading: I've already had many operations — is it worth coming in?

body.text: The number of previous operations alone does not determine the outlook for treatment.
The current condition of the bone, soft tissues, and joints, the presence of infection, and the functional potential of the limb need to be assessed.

blocks.heading: How long does this kind of treatment take?

body.text: With critical defects, treatment can be lengthy and, in complex cases, involve several sequential stages.
Before starting reconstruction, it's important to discuss with the patient not just the planned operations, but also the approximate path from the first stage to functional recovery.

blocks.heading: Can preserving the limb be guaranteed?

body.text: No.
The possibility of reconstruction depends on the severity of the injury, the condition of the vessels, nerves, bone, and soft tissues, infection, and other factors.
During the consultation, it's important to determine the realistic possibilities and risks of reconstructive treatment for the specific patient.

blocks.heading: Losing part of a bone doesn't always mean losing the chance for reconstruction

body.text: If a significant bone defect has formed after an injury, an infection, or previous operations, the first task is to assess whether a stable, functional reconstruction can be achieved, and how to get there.
During the consultation, we'll review your previous treatment, the results of examinations, and the current condition of the limb, and put together a possible reconstructive strategy.
With complex defects, it's important to plan not just the next operation, but the final outcome and the entire path to it.

osteosynthesis.title: Fracture Osteosynthesis
osteosynthesis.lead: Modern surgical treatment of fractures with restoration of anatomy, stable fixation, and a focus on early functional recovery.
osteosynthesis.intro: Not every fracture requires surgery. But if the fragments are significantly displaced, the fracture is unstable, the joint surface is damaged, or conservative treatment cannot maintain the correct position of the bone, osteosynthesis may be necessary.

body.text: Treatment strategy doesn't depend only on which bone is broken.
What matters is the nature of the fracture, displacement of the fragments, stability, the condition of the joint surfaces and soft tissues, the patient's age, and their functional needs.

Some fractures can be successfully treated without surgery. In other cases, without stable surgical fixation it is difficult to restore the correct position of the bone and create optimal conditions for healing.

blocks.heading: When to See a Trauma Orthopedist

items: a displaced fracture has been diagnosed
the fracture extends into a joint
the fragments have shifted again after reduction
the fracture is unstable
there is significant limb deformity
an open fracture has occurred
the fracture is not healing properly
you need to determine whether the fracture can be treated without surgery
surgery has been proposed and you need to understand the possible treatment options

body.text: Osteosynthesis is surgical stabilization of bone fragments in a position that creates conditions for healing and restoration of function.
Various devices can be used for fixation:

items: plates and screws
intramedullary nails
individual screws
wires (K-wires)
external fixators
combinations of different methods

body.text: But choosing the device is only part of the treatment.
The key question is not which plate or nail to use, but which fixation method best matches the specific fracture.
The goal of the operation is to create optimal mechanical and biological conditions for fracture healing.
Depending on the nature of the injury, osteosynthesis makes it possible to:

items: restore the position of the bone fragments
restore the length and axis of the limb
restore the joint surface in intra-articular fractures
provide stability at the fracture site
create conditions for bone healing
in appropriate cases, begin movement earlier
reduce the risk of secondary displacement
gradually return the patient to daily activity

body.text: The goal is not simply to get a good-looking postoperative X-ray, but to restore function of the injured limb.

blocks.heading: Not Every Fracture Needs the Same Fixation

body.text: One of the fundamental features of modern trauma surgery is the ability to use different osteosynthesis methods depending on the specific type of injury.
These allow precise restoration of anatomy and provide stable fixation. They are especially important for many periarticular and intra-articular fractures.
A nail is placed inside the medullary canal and creates stable internal fixation.
This method is widely used for fractures of long bones, particularly the femur and tibia.
In appropriate cases, fixation can be performed through smaller surgical approaches, aiming to minimize additional soft tissue trauma and preserve the biological conditions needed for healing.
This can be used as a temporary or definitive method for certain complex injuries, significant soft tissue damage, and other clinical situations.
The fixation method is chosen to match the fracture — not the fracture adapted to the surgeon's preferred device.

blocks.heading: Special Attention to Fractures Near Joints

body.text: With fractures that extend into the joint surface, the treatment task is more complex than simply joining the bone fragments.
It is necessary to restore, as precisely as possible:

items: the shape of the joint surface
the axis of the limb
stability
anatomical relationships
the potential for future joint movement

body.text: Such fractures require especially careful planning, since incorrect fragment position can affect the future function of the joint.
For simple fractures, standard X-rays may be sufficient.
For complex, multi-fragment, or intra-articular injuries, computed tomography (CT) may additionally be used.
CT allows a more detailed assessment of:

items: the number and position of the fragments
the nature of the joint surface damage
the spatial geometry of the fracture
the possible method of reduction and fixation

body.text: The more complex the fracture geometry, the more important preoperative planning becomes.
We assess the mechanism of injury, the condition of the limb, X-rays, and, if necessary, a CT scan.
We determine the type of fracture, its stability, and the condition of the soft tissues.
We determine whether surgery is needed at all.
If osteosynthesis is indicated, we choose the reduction and fixation method suited to the specific fracture.
The necessary position of the bone fragments is restored and stable fixation is performed.
The extent of the operation depends on the nature of the injury.
After surgery, the range of motion and permitted load are determined.
In some cases, stable fixation allows functional recovery to begin earlier.
Follow-up examinations and X-rays are performed to assess the position of the hardware and the fracture healing process.
As healing progresses, load and physical activity are gradually increased.

blocks.heading: Complex Tibial Fracture After a Motorcycle Fall

body.text: The patient sustained an injury to the right lower leg as a result of a motorcycle fall. Initial X-rays showed a complex, multi-fragment fracture of the distal tibia with displacement of the fragments, combined with a fibula fracture.

Given the nature and location of the injury, a surgical strategy was chosen. The main goals were to restore the axis and anatomical relationships of the limb, achieve stable fixation of the fracture, and create conditions for healing.
Osteosynthesis was performed using an intramedullary nail with additional fixation of the distal fragments.
Follow-up X-rays show a restored tibial axis, maintained fragment position, and stable position of the hardware.
With a complex fracture, it's not enough simply to fix the bone. The method and combination of fixation techniques are chosen to match the specific anatomy of the injury.
Surgical treatment should be used when it offers a real advantage over conservative treatment.
The goal of the consultation is to determine the optimal strategy — not necessarily to lead the patient toward surgery.

blocks.heading: Fixation Method Matched to the Specific Fracture

body.text: A plate, an intramedullary nail, or another fixation method are tools. The choice is determined by the anatomy and mechanics of the specific injury.

blocks.heading: Preserving the Biology of the Fracture

body.text: Stability is important, but preserving the blood supply and soft tissues needed for healing is no less important.

blocks.heading: Thinking About Function from the Start

body.text: When planning surgery, it's important to consider not only the position of the fragments, but also future joint mobility, load-bearing, and the patient's return to daily life.

blocks.heading: Does Every Displaced Fracture Need Surgery?

body.text: No.
The decision depends on the extent and nature of the displacement, the stability of the fracture, its location, and the patient's age and functional needs.
In some cases, an acceptable position can be achieved and maintained without surgery.

blocks.heading: Plate or Intramedullary Nail — Which Is Better?

body.text: There is no universally better method.
These methods have different indications. The choice depends on the location and type of fracture, the condition of the bone and soft tissues, and other factors.

blocks.heading: Does the Hardware Need to Be Removed After Healing?

body.text: No.
If the hardware doesn't cause problems and there are no other indications for removal, a repeat operation is not always necessary.
The decision is made individually.

blocks.heading: When Can I Put Weight on My Leg After Osteosynthesis?

body.text: This depends on the location and nature of the fracture, the stability of the fixation, the quality of the bone tissue, and how healing progresses.
The weight-bearing regimen can vary significantly for different fractures.

blocks.heading: When Should I Start Moving the Joint?

body.text: In many cases, movement is started as early as possible, if the nature of the fracture and the stability of the fixation allow it.
The specific regimen is determined by the surgeon.

blocks.heading: How Long Does It Take for a Fracture to Heal?

body.text: The timeframe depends on the bone, the type of fracture, age, blood supply, the stability of the fixation, and other factors.
So the decision to increase load is made not just according to a calendar, but based on the results of follow-up examinations and X-rays.

blocks.heading: What If the Fracture Doesn't Heal After Surgery?

body.text: First, the cause needs to be determined.
The stability of the hardware, the biological conditions at the fracture site, the presence of a bone defect, the condition of the soft tissues, and other factors are assessed.
After that, the further treatment strategy is determined.

blocks.heading: Can I Get a Second Opinion If Surgery Has Already Been Proposed?

body.text: Yes.
If the situation allows time for a planned decision, we can review the X-rays or CT scan, the proposed strategy, and possible alternatives.

blocks.heading: Do You Have a Fracture and Need to Determine a Treatment Strategy?

body.text: If a complex fracture has been diagnosed, there is significant displacement, or surgery has already been proposed to you, during a consultation we can review the results of your examinations and determine the possible treatment options.
Not every fracture requires surgery. If osteosynthesis is necessary, the main task is to choose the fixation method that will create optimal conditions for healing and functional recovery.

limb-lengthening.title: Height Increase and Aesthetic Limb Lengthening
limb-lengthening.lead: Surgical height increase with individualized planning of body proportions, controlled bone lengthening, and staged functional recovery.
limb-lengthening.intro: Aesthetic limb lengthening allows an increase in height through the gradual lengthening of the thigh bones and/or shin bones.

body.text: This is not a routine cosmetic procedure. The process requires orthopedic planning, surgery, gradual bone lengthening, regular monitoring, and subsequent recovery of limb function.
Yes.
The method is based on the ability of bone tissue to form new bone when it is gradually and controllably lengthened.
During surgery, a controlled osteotomy separates the bone, and a system is installed that allows the distance between the bone fragments to be gradually increased afterward.
New bone tissue gradually forms in the resulting gap.
In this way, limb length is increased not by inserting a "longer bone" or an implant, but through the gradual formation of the patient's own new bone tissue.

blocks.heading: How many centimeters can be added to height?

body.text: This is one of the first questions that comes up when planning aesthetic limb lengthening.
But proper planning does not start with the maximum possible number of centimeters.
Before determining the target lengthening, it is necessary to assess:

items: baseline height
length of the thighs and shins
proportions of the lower limbs and torso
limb axis
condition of the hip, knee, and ankle joints
condition of the bone tissue
joint mobility
the ability of the muscles and other soft tissues to adapt to lengthening
patient expectations

body.text: The goal is not to achieve the maximum number of centimeters at any cost, but to determine a well-founded lengthening that accounts for anatomy, proportions, and safety.
Height increase can be achieved by lengthening the thigh bones (femurs) or the shin bones (tibias).
This is not simply a choice of where to operate.
The thigh and shin have different anatomy, are surrounded by different muscle groups, affect limb proportions differently, and each has its own recovery characteristics.
That is why planning considers not only the desired number of centimeters, but also how lengthening a particular segment will change the body's overall proportions.

In some cases the goal can be achieved by lengthening a single segment. A greater increase in height may require a different strategy and, under the appropriate conditions, separate stages of treatment.
The process consists of several consecutive stages.
We assess the anatomy, segment lengths, lower-limb axis, joint condition, and body proportions.
We discuss the desired outcome and define a realistic, individualized goal.
A controlled osteotomy of the bone is performed, and a system is installed for its subsequent gradual lengthening.
After the initial postoperative period, the gradual lengthening of the bone begins.
The process proceeds in small increments and is monitored with regular check-ups and X-rays.
Once the planned length has been reached, lengthening is stopped.
The newly formed bone tissue gradually matures and gains sufficient strength.
Throughout the entire process, it is important to maintain joint mobility and muscle function.
After lengthening is complete, the gradual restoration of strength, walking, and physical activity continues.

blocks.heading: Internal lengthening nail or external fixator?

body.text: Various technologies exist for bone lengthening.
External fixators have traditionally been used. A modern alternative in certain cases is internal intramedullary lengthening systems, which are placed inside the bone.
The choice of technology depends on:

items: the segment planned for lengthening
bone anatomy
the planned amount of lengthening
the capabilities of the specific system
previous surgeries
individual patient characteristics

body.text: The technology should be selected to fit the treatment plan, not the other way around.
In aesthetic limb lengthening, the final height number is not the only thing that matters.
Changing the length of the thigh or shin changes the ratio between the lower-limb segments and the body's overall proportions.
That is why, even before surgery, it is important to assess how the planned lengthening will affect the patient's appearance and proportions.
In appropriate cases, digital planning allows different lengthening options to be modeled in advance and discussed with the patient.
An aesthetic result is not only about becoming taller, but also about preserving a natural sense of body proportions.

blocks.heading: What happens to the muscles and soft tissues?

body.text: It is not only the bone that is lengthened.
As the segment increases in length, the muscles, tendons, blood vessels, nerves, and other soft tissues gradually adapt.
It is precisely their ability to adapt that is one of the factors determining the acceptable pace and extent of lengthening.
That is why, during treatment, the following are monitored:

items: joint mobility
muscle balance
neurological status
new bone tissue formation
overall limb function

body.text: If necessary, the pace of lengthening can be adjusted.

blocks.heading: Rehabilitation is part of the treatment itself

body.text: In aesthetic limb lengthening, rehabilitation does not begin after treatment is finished.
It is part of the treatment from the very start.
During the lengthening process, it is especially important to maintain mobility of the hip, knee, and ankle joints and to prevent the formation of contractures.
The recovery program changes according to the stage of treatment and includes controlled exercises, work on mobility and muscle function, and a gradual increase in load.

blocks.heading: How long does the entire process take?

body.text: Aesthetic limb lengthening is not a procedure with results in a few weeks.
The full path includes:
preparation → surgery → gradual lengthening → formation and maturation of new bone → functional recovery.
The duration depends on the amount of lengthening, the segment chosen, the technology used, the speed of new bone tissue formation, and the individual course of recovery.
That is why, even before making a decision, the patient should understand not only the expected change in height, but also the time and personal involvement the entire process will require.
We first assess the anatomy, proportions, and condition of the bones and joints. Only after that do we define a well-founded lengthening goal.
Height increase should be evaluated not in isolation, but in the context of the ratio between thigh, shin, and torso length.
Surgery is only the beginning. New bone formation, the condition of soft tissues, joint mobility, and function are monitored throughout the entire lengthening period.

blocks.heading: Safety matters more than the maximum number

body.text: The desire to gain more centimeters is understandable, but increasing the target lengthening simultaneously increases the demands placed on the bone, muscles, nerves, joints, and rehabilitation process.
The patient's motivation may be aesthetic. But the way the result is achieved remains a full-fledged orthopedic reconstructive procedure.
Aesthetic limb lengthening is a serious surgical treatment and carries potential risks.
These may include:

items: delayed new bone tissue formation
restricted joint movement
muscle contractures
pain
sensory disturbances or other neurological symptoms
problems with the fixation device
infectious complications
the need for additional surgical interventions
recovery taking longer than expected

body.text: The risk of complications depends on the amount of lengthening, the method chosen, anatomy, and the individual response of the body.
The decision to undergo aesthetic limb lengthening should be made only after a detailed discussion not only of the desired result, but of the entire process, its limitations, and its possible risks.

blocks.heading: How many centimeters can I realistically gain in height?

body.text: There are technical possibilities for bone lengthening, but there is no universal safe figure for every patient.
The target is determined individually, taking into account the segment, proportions, condition of the soft tissues and joints, and other factors.

blocks.heading: Can I simply say, "I want +10 cm"?

body.text: This can be stated as a desired goal, but it should not automatically become the surgical plan.
It must first be assessed whether this amount of lengthening is well-founded for the specific anatomy, and by what path it could potentially be achieved.

blocks.heading: Which is better to lengthen — the thighs or the shins?

body.text: There is no universal answer.
The choice depends on the baseline proportions, anatomy, the desired amount of height increase, and the capabilities of the specific technology.

blocks.heading: Can both the thighs and the shins be lengthened?

body.text: There are strategies that involve lengthening different segments, but the necessity, sequence, and permissible extent of such procedures require separate planning.
The surgery and the gradual lengthening process can be accompanied by pain and discomfort.
The intensity of sensations changes at different stages and varies between patients. Pain management and adjusting the treatment pace are part of the medical care provided.

blocks.heading: Will I be able to walk during lengthening?

body.text: The ability to walk and the permissible level of weight-bearing depend on the device used, the segment, the stage of treatment, and how new bone formation is progressing.
The walking regimen is determined individually and may change over the course of treatment.
Any surgical procedure leaves postoperative scars.
Their number and location depend on the technology chosen. Scars change over time, but it is impossible to guarantee they will become completely unnoticeable.

blocks.heading: When can I return to work?

body.text: This depends on the nature of the work, the lengthening method used, and the stage of treatment.
Remote or sedentary work and physically demanding professional activity require fundamentally different return timelines.

blocks.heading: When can I return to sports?

body.text: A return to sports activity follows sufficient maturation of the new bone tissue and restoration of limb strength, mobility, and control.
This is one of the later stages of recovery.
During the lengthening process itself, gait temporarily changes.
One of the goals of rehabilitation after treatment is complete is to restore a normal walking pattern and adapt to the new limb length.

blocks.heading: Can I first simply find out what result is possible in my case?

body.text: Yes.
A consultation does not mean committing to surgery.

Its purpose is to assess your anatomy and proportions, discuss the desired result, possible technologies, the approximate treatment path, and determine whether aesthetic limb lengthening is a suitable option for you.

blocks.heading: Want to find out how much your height could be increased?

body.text: The first step is not surgery, but individualized planning.

During a consultation, we can assess the proportions of your body and lower limbs, discuss the desired change in height, possible segments for lengthening, technology, treatment duration, and the main limitations.
The goal of the consultation is to determine not the maximum number of centimeters, but a realistic and well-founded height-increase option for your specific anatomy.

revision-arthroplasty.title: Revision Arthroplasty
revision-arthroplasty.lead: Repeat surgery on the hip and knee for implant loosening, wear, instability, fractures, and other complications after primary arthroplasty.
revision-arthroplasty.intro: If pain has returned after your joint replacement, walking has become more difficult, you feel instability in the joint, or your doctor has recommended another operation, the first step is always to determine the cause of the problem.

body.text: Revision arthroplasty is often more complex than the original operation and requires detailed preoperative planning.

blocks.heading: Why an implant may need a repeat operation

body.text: Modern joint replacement can restore joint function for many years, but no artificial construct lasts forever.
A repeat operation may be needed many years after the primary arthroplasty, or much sooner, if a complication develops.
The reasons can vary:

items: aseptic loosening of the components
wear of the implant's parts
dislocation or instability
periprosthetic fracture
significant bone loss
malpositioning of the components
mechanical failure of the construct
infectious complications
other causes of pain and impaired function after arthroplasty

body.text: It is the underlying cause that determines the further treatment approach.
So pain after joint replacement does not automatically mean the entire implant needs to be replaced.

blocks.heading: Your implant hurts — does that mean it needs to be replaced?

body.text: Not necessarily.
Pain after joint replacement can have many different origins. Not every cause is related to loosening of the components, and not every case requires revision surgery.
Before any decision is made, it's important to answer several questions:

items: What exactly is the source of the pain?
Are the implant components stable?
Are they correctly positioned?
Are there signs of infection?
What is the condition of the bone around the implant?
Are there other causes of impaired function?

body.text: Only after answering these questions can we determine whether surgery is needed and, if so, what its scope should be.
Over time, one or more components of an implant can lose stable fixation to the bone.
A patient may experience pain during walking and weight-bearing, a gradual decline in function, or a sense that the joint no longer works the way it used to.
X-rays and other studies are used to assess the stability of the components and the condition of the surrounding bone.
If clinically significant loosening is confirmed, revision arthroplasty may become necessary.
Over long-term use, an implant's components can gradually wear.
In some cases, wear particles can trigger a reaction in the surrounding tissue and lead to a gradual loss of bone — a process known as osteolysis.
This process can progress for a long time without producing noticeable symptoms.
That's why, many years after joint replacement, periodic X-ray monitoring can be important even when the implant still seems to be functioning well.
One of the possible complications after hip replacement is dislocation.
A single episode does not always mean revision surgery is needed.
But with recurrent dislocations, the underlying cause must be identified.
It may be related to component positioning, the condition of the soft tissues, joint mechanics, or a combination of several factors.
In this situation, revision surgery should be aimed at eliminating the cause of the instability — not simply reducing the joint one more time.
A fracture of the bone near an existing implant is a distinct and complex orthopedic trauma problem.
To choose the right treatment, it's important to determine:

items: the location and nature of the fracture
the stability of the implant components
the quality of the bone
the presence of a bone defect
the patient's overall condition

body.text: In some situations, osteosynthesis is possible while keeping a stable implant in place.
In others, one or more components need to be replaced using revision systems.
So a periprosthetic fracture requires treating both the fracture itself and the stability of the implant at the same time.
Periprosthetic infection is fundamentally different from mechanical loosening.
Choosing the right approach requires confirming or ruling out an infectious process and assessing its nature.

Depending on the clinical situation, treatment may involve different strategies — from surgical debridement with retention of the components in selected cases, to single- or two-stage revision arthroplasty.
With a two-stage strategy, treatment can include:
removal of the infected components ↓ surgical debridement ↓ placement of a temporary spacer ↓ control of the infectious process ↓ repeat joint replacement
The approach is determined individually for each patient.

blocks.heading: How revision surgery differs from the primary joint replacement

body.text: Revision arthroplasty is often technically more demanding.

The surgeon works with anatomy that has already been altered. Previous surgical approaches, scar tissue, existing components, possible bone loss, and the condition of the soft tissues all have to be taken into account.
During the operation, it may be necessary to:

items: remove one or more components
preserve any components that remain stable and suitable
remove cement or other materials
reconstruct bone defects
restore a stable foundation for the new implant
use specialized revision components
restore the limb's length, stability, and biomechanics

body.text: Revision surgery is not simply "putting in a new implant instead of the old one." It's a reconstruction of the joint under anatomical conditions that have already changed.
One of the main challenges in complex revision arthroplasty is a shortage of bone.
It can result from loosening, osteolysis, infection, fracture, or previous operations.
Before revision surgery, it's important to assess:

items: the location of the defect
its size
the quality of the remaining bone
the options for fixing the new component

body.text: Depending on the situation, treatment may involve specialized revision components, bone grafting, augments, and other reconstructive solutions.
In the most complex cases, individual planning and patient-specific implants may be needed.

blocks.heading: Does the entire implant need to be replaced?

body.text: Not always.
Revision arthroplasty does not necessarily mean replacing every component.
If part of the construct remains stable, correctly positioned, and compatible with the reconstruction plan, it can be preserved in appropriate cases.
In other cases, a full revision is necessary.
The scope of surgery is determined by the reason the primary arthroplasty failed and by the condition of each component individually.

blocks.heading: How preparation for revision arthroplasty works
01 — Reviewing the history of the primary operation

body.text: When was the joint replacement performed? Which implant was used? How did recovery go? When did the symptoms appear?
If you still have discharge summaries, operative reports, or information about the model of implant used, it's best to bring them to the consultation.
We assess the position of the components, their stability, the condition of the surrounding bone, and any changes compared with earlier studies.
Older X-rays can be especially useful, as they allow us to see how the problem has developed over time.
Depending on the situation, a CT scan, laboratory tests, and other diagnostic methods may be needed.
A separate priority is to rule out or confirm infection.
We determine which components need to be replaced, which can be preserved, how large a bone defect needs to be reconstructed, and which implants may be required.
The planned reconstruction is carried out using the necessary revision components and methods for restoring bone support.
Your weight-bearing regimen and rehabilitation depend on the scope of the revision, the condition of the bone, and the stability of the reconstruction.

blocks.heading: We start by establishing the cause

body.text: Pain after joint replacement is a symptom, not a diagnosis.
Before a repeat operation, it's essential to pinpoint as precisely as possible why the primary arthroplasty stopped providing the expected function.

blocks.heading: We plan the revision before we ever reach the operating room

body.text: How complex a revision arthroplasty will be is often determined well before the operation begins.
Analyzing X-rays, CT scans, previous surgeries, and the type of implant in place allows us to prepare possible reconstructive solutions in advance.

blocks.heading: We preserve what can be preserved

body.text: Not every component needs to be automatically removed.
If a component is stable and preserving it fits the overall surgical plan, that can be part of the chosen strategy.
During a revision, the surgeon must be ready not only to replace the implant, but also to reconstruct the bone support needed to fix it stably.

blocks.heading: We combine arthroplasty with reconstructive orthopedics

body.text: Especially complex revisions can require methods that go beyond standard primary arthroplasty: bone defect reconstruction, specialized revision systems, and individualized planning.

blocks.heading: A second opinion before revision surgery
Have you been told your implant needs to be replaced?

body.text: With revision arthroplasty, the decision can be far more complex than it was for the primary operation.
Before another procedure, it's important to understand:

items: why the problem occurred
whether revision is really necessary
which components need to be replaced
whether part of the implant can be preserved
whether there is a bone defect
whether infection has been ruled out
what scope of reconstruction may be needed

body.text: If a repeat operation has already been proposed to you, a second opinion lets you independently assess the cause of the problem and the possible revision options before making a final decision.

blocks.heading: How long does an implant last?

body.text: There is no universal timeframe after which an implant must be replaced.
How long it lasts depends on the type of construct, the method of fixation, the load placed on it, the condition of the bone, and many other factors.
The age of the implant on its own is not an indication for revision.

blocks.heading: If my implant is 15–20 years old, should it be replaced as a precaution?

body.text: Not necessarily.
If it's stable, functioning well, and there's no significant wear or osteolysis, the decision to operate is usually not based on age alone.
At the same time, routine follow-up X-rays can catch changes before significant symptoms appear.

blocks.heading: Why did my implant start hurting after several years?

body.text: There can be many reasons — from problems directly involving the components to conditions affecting the surrounding tissues or other structures.
That's exactly why diagnosing the cause of the pain is essential before any revision is considered.

blocks.heading: Can loosening be seen on a standard X-ray?

body.text: In many cases, X-rays provide important information about the condition of the implant and the surrounding bone.
But sometimes additional imaging is needed to clarify the picture.

blocks.heading: Can only one component be replaced?

body.text: In certain situations — yes.
If the other components are stable, correctly positioned, and compatible with the planned reconstruction, a partial revision can be considered.

blocks.heading: What should I do if my implant has dislocated?

body.text: The first priority is to restore the correct position of the joint and assess the cause of the dislocation.
Revision is not always needed after a first episode. With recurrent instability, a more detailed workup is required.

blocks.heading: Is a second operation more difficult than the first?

body.text: Often — yes.
During a revision, the surgeon works with altered anatomy, scar tissue, previously implanted components, and possible bone loss.
That's why preoperative planning becomes especially important.

blocks.heading: Can an implant be reinserted after an infection?

body.text: In many clinical situations — yes.
But the approach depends on the nature of the infection, the condition of the bone and soft tissues, and the results of the earlier treatment.

blocks.heading: Can a third or fourth operation be performed on the same joint?

body.text: The number of previous operations, on its own, doesn't determine whether another revision is possible.
What matters more is the condition of the bone and soft tissues, the stability of the construct, the presence of infection, and the options remaining for further reconstruction.

blocks.heading: What documents should I bring to the consultation?

body.text: It's best to bring:

items: your most recent X-rays
earlier X-rays, if you still have them
discharge summaries from the primary operation and any subsequent procedures
information about the implant that was used
CT and laboratory results, if these have already been done

body.text: Even old studies can be very useful, since they help us assess how the situation has changed over time.
Pain, instability, or changes seen on an X-ray don't always mean the entire implant needs to be replaced right away.
The first step is to establish the cause of the problem and assess the condition of the existing components and the surrounding bone.
During a consultation, we can review your previous treatment, X-rays, and other tests, and outline the possible options going forward.
If revision arthroplasty has already been recommended to you, the consultation can also serve as an opportunity to get a second opinion before you go ahead with another operation.

3d-implants.title: Custom 3D-printed implants
3d-implants.lead: Personalized reconstructive solutions for complex orthopedic cases where a standard implant is not enough.
3d-implants.intro: After a severe injury, significant bone loss, or several previous operations, the anatomy can change so much that standard off-the-shelf implants no longer offer the best solution to the reconstructive problem.

body.text: In such cases, modern CT imaging, digital 3D planning, and additive manufacturing make it possible to design a custom implant tailored to the anatomy of a specific patient.

blocks.heading: When a standard solution may not be enough

body.text: Most orthopedic operations are successfully carried out using off-the-shelf implants in standard sizes.
But there are clinical situations in which the surgeon is not dealing with standard anatomy.
This can be caused by:

items: a significant post-traumatic bone defect
loss of part of the bone after an infection
the consequences of multi-stage surgical treatment
pronounced post-traumatic deformity
anatomy altered by previous operations
a complex defect near a joint
the need to replace a missing bone fragment
a situation where a standard construct doesn't match the geometry of the specific defect

body.text: In such cases, one possible solution is to design a construct for the specific patient, rather than adapting the patient to an available standard implant.
It is an implant whose geometry is designed to match the anatomy and specific reconstructive needs of a single patient.
It is based on computed tomography.
A digital three-dimensional model of the bone is built from the CT scan. It allows a detailed assessment of the defect, its spatial geometry, and how the anatomical structures relate to one another.
From there, the future reconstruction can be planned and the shape and parameters of the needed construct determined.
In other words, we first build a digital model of the planned reconstruction — and only then design the implant to carry it out.

blocks.heading: From CT scan to custom implant

body.text: A CT scan of the relevant segment is performed following the appropriate protocol.
The quality of this initial data is critical, since it becomes the foundation for all subsequent digital modeling.
A digital model of the bone is created from the CT scan.
It allows us to see the defect in three dimensions and assess its geometry in far more detail than a standard X-ray allows.
We determine which anatomy needs to be restored, the position of the future construct, how it will interact with the remaining bone, and the possible fixation options.
In appropriate cases, the anatomy of the healthy opposite limb can be used as a reference for the reconstruction.
A digital model of the custom implant is created based on the surgical plan.
At this stage, the surgical and engineering sides of the process effectively merge.
Once the final design is approved, the construct is manufactured using the appropriate additive manufacturing technology, from a material intended for medical use.
The implant is used as part of the reconstruction that was planned in advance.
In this way, the operation doesn't begin in the operating room — much of a complex reconstruction is planned well before the surgery itself.
The main advantage of a personalized construct isn't simply the use of 3D printing.
Its purpose is to help solve a specific anatomical problem.
Depending on the clinical situation, a custom solution can make it possible to:

items: recreate the complex geometry of a missing fragment
adapt the construct to the remaining bone
plan the required position of the implant in advance
restore limb length and anatomical relationships
determine possible fixation points ahead of time
carry out a reconstruction for which no standard implant is sufficient

body.text: 3D technology is not the goal of treatment. Its value lies in the ability to carry out the reconstructive plan for a specific patient.

blocks.heading: A custom implant isn't always the first stage

body.text: With complex post-traumatic defects, the final reconstruction can't always be performed right away.
If infection, nonviable tissue, instability, or other issues are present, a preparatory stage of treatment may be needed first.
The overall strategy may look like this:

removal of nonviable or infected tissue ↓ control of the local situation ↓ temporary stabilization or defect replacement ↓ CT scan and digital planning of the final reconstruction ↓ manufacturing of the custom implant ↓ final reconstruction
So a custom implant should be viewed as part of an overall reconstructive strategy, not as a standalone technology product.

blocks.heading: Why the healthy limb is sometimes used

body.text: With a complex unilateral defect, part of the normal anatomy may be completely lost.
In such situations, a CT scan of the healthy opposite limb can be used to create its mirrored digital model.
This gives us a reference for what the original anatomy of the injured segment likely looked like before the injury.
The model is then adapted to the specific reconstructive task.
In effect, the healthy side can become the anatomical template for digitally restoring the injured one.
Creating a custom implant is a team process.
An engineer can design a complex construct, but it's the surgeon who determines:

items: what needs to be restored
what the final anatomy should look like
where the implant can be positioned
how it will be inserted
how fixation should be achieved
how the construct fits into the overall surgical plan

body.text: That's why digital design happens through an ongoing exchange between clinical and engineering planning.

blocks.heading: The reconstructive problem comes first — the technology second

body.text: We don't start with the question "can a 3D implant be printed?"
We first determine exactly what needs to be restored, and whether a custom construct genuinely offers an advantage over standard methods.

blocks.heading: We plan the operation in a digital environment

body.text: The 3D model allows us to assess complex anatomy and part of the planned reconstruction before we ever reach the operating room.
A custom construct isn't created separately from the operation — it's built to match a specific surgical plan.

blocks.heading: We consider the whole course of treatment

body.text: When a multi-stage reconstruction is needed, each stage has to set up the conditions for the next one.

blocks.heading: We don't use 3D printing where a standard solution is enough

body.text: A custom solution is justified when it helps solve a problem that would be difficult or impossible to address optimally with standard means.

blocks.heading: Custom 3D reconstruction of a significant post-traumatic tibial defect

body.text: In complex post-traumatic cases, custom 3D planning makes it possible to move from assessing the defect to creating a personalized construct and carrying out a reconstruction that was planned in advance.
The website presents a real clinical case of reconstructing a significant tibial defect using a custom 3D-printed implant, along with the long-term functional outcome.

blocks.heading: Can a 3D implant be made for any defect?

body.text: The technical ability to create a custom construct doesn't necessarily mean it will be the best treatment option.
The defect, the condition of the bone and soft tissues, the presence of infection, and possible standard reconstruction options all need to be assessed first.

blocks.heading: How does a custom implant differ from a standard one?

body.text: A standard implant is mass-produced in a defined range of shapes and sizes.
A custom construct is designed for the specific anatomy and specific reconstructive needs of a single patient.

blocks.heading: What material are these implants made from?

body.text: The material depends on the type of construct and its purpose. Custom orthopedic implants may be made from biocompatible metal materials, including titanium alloys.
The specific material is determined during the design and manufacturing of the construct.

blocks.heading: Why is a CT scan necessary?

body.text: A CT scan is the basis for creating an accurate three-dimensional model of the bone.
A standard X-ray remains important for assessing the limb, but personalized 3D design requires spatially accurate digital data about the anatomy.

blocks.heading: Why is a CT scan sometimes needed for both limbs?

body.text: If the defect is unilateral and part of the normal anatomy is lost, the healthy opposite side can serve as a reference.
Its digital model is mirrored and used to help reconstruct the missing anatomy.

blocks.heading: How long does it take to manufacture a custom implant?

body.text: This is not a ready-made product taken off a shelf.
A CT scan needs to be performed, a 3D model created, a surgical plan formed, the construct designed, approved, and then manufactured.
The time required depends on the complexity of the case and the manufacturing process, and is determined individually.

blocks.heading: Can a custom implant be placed immediately after an injury?

body.text: Not always.
With a complex injury, the initial priorities may be stabilization, removal of nonviable tissue, soft-tissue reconstruction, and infection control.
The final custom reconstruction is carried out once the right conditions for it have been established.

blocks.heading: Can a 3D implant replace a large missing piece of bone?

body.text: In certain clinical situations, custom constructs can be part of the reconstruction of significant bone defects.
Whether this treatment is possible is determined after assessing the specific defect and the entire limb.

blocks.heading: Is this better than bone grafting?

body.text: Not necessarily.

These are different reconstructive tools with different indications. In some cases, a biological reconstruction is the best option; in others, a custom construct or a combination of methods works better.

blocks.heading: What should I do if I've been told there's no standard implant for my case?

body.text: The absence of a suitable standard implant doesn't automatically mean a 3D construct is needed.
In a complex situation, it's worth reviewing the CT scan, previous operations, and possible reconstructive options — including getting a second opinion on the best course of treatment.

blocks.heading: Is a standard solution not enough for you?

body.text: If, after an injury, loss of part of the bone, or several previous operations, you've been told that a standard construct can't solve the problem, it's worth exploring the options for a custom reconstruction.
During the consultation, we'll review your test results and previous treatment and determine whether a custom 3D solution offers an advantage in your specific clinical situation.
A custom implant is not the goal of treatment. The goal is to find the reconstructive approach that best matches your specific anatomy and functional needs.
